### ATLAS-IMP-279 Scope and Verification

#### ATLAS-041 Reasoning -- complete, 15/15 slices

- **Slice 1 -- epistemic types and evidence unit** (`backend/src/atlas/modules/reasoning/domain/models.py`): `EpistemicType` (SS4's nine types) is a fresh taxonomy, not a reuse of Guardrails' `ClaimType` -- SS4 splits `ClaimType.FACT` into `OBSERVATION` (direct time-stamped source/connector result) and `RETRIEVED_FACT` (cited governed-source statement), and adds `RECOMMENDATION`, which `ClaimType` has no equivalent for; `ClaimType` itself is left untouched since Explainability's shipped `ExplanationClaim` already depends on it. `EvidenceUnit` covers SS5's ten declared elements; `can_support_a_consequential_claim` notes that scope/time/provenance/access are already guaranteed present by the dataclass's own required fields, so the property only has integrity and completeness left to check. 15 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project) clean.
- **Slice 2 -- claim contract** (`domain/claims.py`): `ConfidenceCategory` (SS18's five categories, defined here since SS6's claim contract needs it before SS18's own slice builds the fuller structured confidence assessment) and `ReasoningClaim` covering SS6's ten elements. `requires_supporting_evidence`/`ReasoningClaim.is_evidence_gap` mirror Explainability's `ExplanationClaim.is_evidence_gap` "construct-then-evaluate" pattern -- a claim of an evidence-required epistemic type with no evidence is still constructible, exposed as a checkable gap rather than blocked at construction. `__post_init__` enforces a disputed claim requires reviewer feedback, and `superseded_by_claim_id` can be present if and only if `lifecycle_state is SUPERSEDED` -- SS6's "claims can be superseded ... without rewriting historical reasoning" given a real, checkable shape. 23 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and both reasoning test files (38 total) clean.
- **Slice 3 -- problem framing** (`domain/framing.py`): `ProblemFrame` covers SS8's nine declared elements, reusing `atlas.core.capabilities.CapabilityClass` and slice 2's `ConfidenceCategory` rather than new enums. SS8's "ambiguous target identity, mixed environments, or incompatible time windows are resolved or disclosed before analysis" gets a real, populated home in `ambiguity_disclosures` (a typed `FramingAmbiguityDisclosure` list, one member per kind, each requiring non-blank text) rather than an unstated convention -- a caller who found ambiguity has a concrete place to record it, and `has_disclosed_ambiguity` gives that state a checkable call site. 11 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all reasoning test files (49 total) clean.
- **Slice 4 -- evidence quality** (`domain/quality.py`): `EvidenceQualityAssessment` gives SS10's "a single aggregate quality score must not hide one critical weakness" real teeth by absence -- the type has no aggregate/overall score field at all, only a per-dimension breakdown across SS10's nine named dimensions, so nothing in this type can even represent the thing SS10 forbids. `weakest_dimensions` surfaces every `WEAK`-rated dimension explicitly, directly matching SS10's own worked example (authoritative vendor guidance that's still inapplicable to the installed version) as a concrete test case. An assessment may rate any subset of the nine dimensions -- not every dimension is knowable for every piece of evidence, so completeness is not required. 8 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all reasoning test files (57 total) clean.
- **Slice 5 -- temporal reasoning** (`domain/temporal.py`): reuses Explainability's `ClockQuality` (`investigation_presentation.py`) directly for "clock quality and known skew are visible" rather than a second scale. `TemporalEvent` distinguishes occurrence/observation/ingestion/report times (SS11's four times); `has_conflicting_timestamps` checks the times are in the order they must physically follow, giving "conflicting timestamps reduce certainty" a real, computable signal. `observation_order_proves_causation` is a hardcoded `False`, a concrete call site for "later observation does not prove later causation." `is_temporally_current` takes `now` explicitly (this codebase's established freshness-check convention) and always has a reference time to check against, since `reported_at` is a required field and the guaranteed fallback when observation/occurrence times are unknown. 15 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all reasoning test files (72 total) clean.
- **Slice 6 -- graph and dependency reasoning** (`domain/graph_reasoning.py`): reuses `graph.domain.models.RelationshipType` and `AssertionMethod` directly -- ATLAS-026 already supplies the time-aware entities/relationships SS12 reasons over -- and adds only what's missing: `RelationshipNature` (physical/logical/service/ownership/inferred, an axis orthogonal to `RelationshipType`), `GraphTraversalScope`/`is_within_traversal_scope` for SS12's authorized-scope and depth/expansion bounds, and `DependencyClaim` for the rest (type/direction/source/observation-time, `is_active_dependency` as a field genuinely distinct from mere graph reachability, alternative paths/redundancy/shared dependencies, and a required `graph_evidence_citation` for "cite graph evidence used for impact or causality claims"). `is_low_confidence` flags SS12's "expose missing or low-confidence relationships" using slice 2's `ConfidenceCategory`. 16 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all reasoning test files (88 total) clean.
- **Slice 7 -- hypothesis ledger and generation** (`domain/hypotheses.py`): `ReasoningHypothesis` covers SS13's nine elements; `reason_for_state_change` can be present if and only if `state is not PROPOSED` -- every state beyond the initial one is itself a change, so the invariant is symmetric rather than picking specific "changed" states to enumerate. A `CONFIRMED` hypothesis additionally requires supporting evidence. `active_hypotheses` implements "Atlas keeps multiple plausible hypotheses until evidence discriminates among them" by excluding only `REJECTED` (a `CONFIRMED` hypothesis is the resolved answer, not something to discard). `satisfies_diversity_requirement` implements SS14's "bounded and diverse enough to avoid fixation," scaling the diversity requirement down when fewer hypotheses exist than the configured minimum -- a single hypothesis cannot itself be "diverse." 16 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all reasoning test files (104 total) clean.
- **Slice 8 -- discriminating checks** (`domain/discriminating_checks.py`): `DiscriminatingCheck` covers SS15's bounded-target/duration/load/output/data-exposure elements, requiring at least two `ExpectedResultUnderHypothesis` entries -- a check that can't discriminate between at least two hypotheses isn't discriminating. `is_within_capability_ceiling` is a standalone function (not a stored field) comparing the check's own capability class against the task's ceiling from `ProblemFrame` (slice 3), mirroring Runbook Engine's `branch_broadens_capability_class` pattern. `CheckRankingFactors`/`rank_checks` implement "Atlas ranks checks by information gain, safety, freshness, cost, and time, using deterministic support where feasible" as a plain, deterministic weighted sum over normalized [0.0, 1.0] factors. "Does not repeat already sufficient evidence without reason" is stated as an honest gap: it needs caller-level context (what a check's expected evidence overlaps with already-sufficient evidence) this object's own shape doesn't carry. 14 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all reasoning test files (118 total) clean.
- **Slice 9 -- causal reasoning rules and counterfactual analysis** (`domain/causal_reasoning.py`): `CausalAssertion` gives two SS16 rules real teeth structurally -- a `CORRELATION`-typed assertion cannot also set `asserts_root_cause` ("correlation is not labeled root cause"), and `confirmation_criteria` can be present if and only if `is_confirmed_cause` ("confirmed cause requires domain-defined evidence and validation criteria"). `temporal_precedence_alone_proves_causation`/`recent_change_alone_proves_causation` are hardcoded `False`; `recovery_strengthens_hypothesis` requires both alternative-causes and coincident-recovery to be considered. `HumanConfirmation` has no field through which a confirmation could be marked infallible -- "preserved as evidence ... not as infallible truth" enforced by the absence of such a field, not a check against one. `CounterfactualStatement` (SS17) ties `supporting_reference` to any `basis` other than `ESTIMATE`, giving "labeled as estimates unless supported by a validated simulator or historical experiment" a structural guarantee. 22 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all reasoning test files (140 total) clean.
- **Slice 10 -- confidence representation and updating** (`domain/confidence.py`): `ConfidenceAssessment` covers SS18's supporting/reducing-factors/unknowns/what-would-change-it elements, tying `numeric_score` to a required `numeric_score_calibration_reference` -- "numeric scores are used only after calibration against domain datasets" as a construct-time guarantee. `is_independent_support`/`support_weight_for` implement SS19's duplicate-evidence and staleness/applicability discounting as real computations rather than boolean conventions. `ContradictionRecord` has no averaged/reconciled field at all -- only the two contradicting sides preserved separately -- so "contradictory authoritative evidence ... cannot be averaged away" is enforced by absence, matching slice 4's `EvidenceQualityAssessment` pattern. `approval_can_increase_confidence` is a hardcoded `False`; `absence_of_alert_is_evidence` requires both alert coverage and system health to be known. - **Slice 7 -- decision caching** (`domain/decision_cache.py`): SS19's `PolicyDecisionCacheKey` (policy-set versions, actor, operation, target, parameter digest -- everything SS19 says Allow caching requires, applied uniformly to Deny too since that is strictly safer) and an in-memory `PolicyDecisionCache` (get/put/invalidate_for_actor/invalidate_all), TTL-bound and evicting expired entries outright rather than just hiding them. `put` validates the cached decision's own actor/operation actually match its key, catching a real class of cache-poisoning bug rather than trusting the caller. Deliberately does not attempt SS19's fine-grained "connector, approval, security, or target-state changes invalidate decisions" wiring -- only the coarse `invalidate_for_actor` primitive a caller can build on, since the finer-grained triggers depend on modules (connectors, security) this cache has no reason to import. 11 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all eight Policy Engine test files (127 total) clean.
- **Slice 8 -- policy lifecycle transitions and authoring separation** (`domain/lifecycle.py`): SS15 lists the ten lifecycle states but draws no transition diagram between them -- this module's own design, documented as such rather than presented as lifted from the spec: draft -> validating -> simulation -> review -> approved -> (scheduled ->) active -> suspended/deprecated -> retired, with fallback-to-draft paths from validating/simulation/review. `require_authoring_separation` enforces SS22's "one identity cannot author and approve the same material permission expansion." 16 new tests, including one that iterates every `PolicyLifecycleState` to catch a future state addition nobody wired a transition for. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all nine Policy Engine test files (142 total) clean.
- **Slice 9 -- simulation service** (`domain/simulation.py`): `simulate_policy` runs curated `SimulationCase`s (SS17's "curated allow and deny cases", generic enough to also express its other six named categories) through the already-pure `evaluate_policy` and reports pass/fail against each case's expected outcome; `find_outcome_regressions` runs the same cases against both a baseline and a candidate policy set and reports which case outcomes would change -- SS16's "before and after semantic diff" applied to real cases rather than rule text. "Simulation never authorizes or executes the represented operations" (SS17) holds trivially, since `evaluate_policy` has no side effect to begin with. 8 new tests, including one proving only genuinely-changed cases are reported, not every case touched by a rule change. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all ten Policy Engine test files (149 total) clean.
- **Slice 10 -- mandatory-test activation gate** (`domain/lifecycle.py` + `domain/simulation.py`): SS18's "a policy package cannot activate with failing mandatory deny tests," wired as the combination of slices 8 and 9 rather than a new concept -- added a `mandatory: bool` flag to `SimulationCase`/`SimulationCaseResult` (propagated through `simulate_policy`) and `SimulationResult.mandatory_failures`, then `lifecycle.require_mandatory_tests_pass` raises when transitioning into SCHEDULED or ACTIVE (both are activations SS18's gate applies to) while any mandatory case still fails; every other lifecycle state is ungated, so a candidate can fail every test and still sit in REVIEW. 9 new tests, including a parametrized check that all eight non-activating states are never gated. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all eleven Policy Engine test files (162 total) clean.
- **Slice 11 -- break-glass emergency procedure** (`domain/break_glass.py`): `BreakGlassRecord` makes SS21's seven requirements real fields (named human identity, authentication method, justification, incident reference, narrow target/capability/duration, independent notification) rather than a free-text blob one of them could hide inside; `apply_break_glass_override` can only ever override an ordinary policy-set-driven denial, never a non-overridable one -- SS21 names the C5-autonomous-execution prohibition specifically as one break-glass cannot weaken, and this applies that principle to all ten non-overridable rules uniformly, not just that one. C5 itself is not banned from break-glass: since the record structurally requires a named human and strong authentication, it can never represent "autonomous" execution in the first place, so the non-overridable check alone already does the real work. 15 new tests covering a successful override, every refusal path (non-overridable denial, target/capability mismatch, not-yet-active, expired), and the record's own field validation. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all twelve Policy Engine test files (174 total) clean.
- **Slice 12 -- policy explanation** (`domain/explanation.py`): `explain_decision` projects a `PolicyDecision` into SS26's user-safe shape (outcome, reasons, a required next step per outcome, decision identifier) -- a safe projection, not a filter, since `PolicyDecision` never carried anything SS26 says must stay hidden (no untriggered rule content, no other identity's data, no secrets) to begin with. Stated plainly rather than fabricated: `PolicyDecision` still has no validity-interval/expiry field (SS8 lists one), so SS26's "expiry where relevant" isn't fulfilled yet. Caught and fixed a real test bug of its own during this slice: a parametrized "every outcome" test tried to build a bare DENY decision with zero reasons, which `PolicyDecision`'s own slice-1 invariant correctly rejects -- fixed the test, not the invariant. 8 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all thirteen Policy Engine test files (189 total) clean.
- **Slice 13 -- decision audit** (`application/audit.py`): `record_policy_decision` maps a `PolicyDecision` onto `atlas.core.audit`'s already-built `AuditRecord`/`AuditSink` -- the same primitive `authorization`'s own service already records through -- rather than building a second, Policy Engine-specific audit path. A `_result_code` helper distinguishes non-overridable denial, rule-driven denial, deny-by-default, allow, and condition-required into stable, queryable codes. Scoped to decision auditing only (what earlier slices can actually produce); SS24 also requires auditing policy lifecycle events and break-glass use, left to whatever application service eventually owns those administrative actions since this module has no such event of its own to record. 7 new tests using a recording fake `AuditSink`. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all fourteen Policy Engine test files (196 total) clean.
- **Slice 14 -- fail-closed failure handling, completing Policy Engine** (`domain/failure.py`): `deny_for_failure` is the single well-formed DENY every one of SS20's seven failure rows resolves to (policy store unavailable, evaluation error, unknown policy version, context/approval-service unavailable, audit unavailable, clock uncertainty) -- one construction site, not one per caller. `evaluate_policy_safely` wraps "fetch policy sets, evaluate" so any exception from either step is caught and converted, never propagated and never silently defaulting to Allow. 5 new tests, including one that patches `evaluate_policy` itself to force a genuine evaluation-error path (the function cannot naturally raise for well-typed input, so this is the honest way to exercise that branch) and one confirming a real deny-by-default decision is distinguishable from a failure-path deny by its reason text. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all fifteen Policy Engine test files (201 total) clean. **This completes ATLAS-025 Policy Engine's 14 planned slices** -- domain model, versioned store, evaluation engine, default capability matrix, approval binding, evidence conditions, caching, lifecycle/authoring separation, simulation, the mandatory-test gate, break-glass, explanation, audit, and fail-closed handling, each independently tested and verified against the real toolchain.

### ATLAS-047 Guardrails -- in progress

- **Slice 1 -- invariant registry and decision contract** (`backend/src/atlas/modules/guardrails/domain/models.py`): `GuardrailClass` (SS7's four configuration postures), `GuardrailInvariant` (all 16 GRD-001 through GRD-016, using the document's own identifiers as enum values so a decision's `rule_id` can reference one directly), a summary for each, `GuardrailOutcome` (SS26's six outcomes), and `GuardrailDecision` (SS26's exact decision contract). Enforces one real, defensible invariant of its own: an `INVARIANT`-class decision can only be `pass` or `block` -- SS7's own table says an invariant "must always hold; violation stops operation," which is inherently binary, not a five-outcome spectrum. 24 tests, including exhaustive coverage of every invariant having a summary and the GRD-NNN identifier set matching the document exactly. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project) clean.
- **Slice 2 -- instruction hierarchy** (`domain/instruction_hierarchy.py`): `InstructionSource` (SS9's six-level precedence as an `IntEnum`, 1=platform invariant through 6=retrieved/tool content), `effective_source` (always returns the real governed channel, never a claimed one -- there is no code path where a claim wins, which is the control itself), and `can_override`/`require_no_precedence_violation` enforcing "lower-level content cannot modify higher-level controls." **Caught a real bug via its own test suite**: the first `can_override` draft had the comparison direction backwards (`acting_source.value >= target_source.value`, which would have let *weaker* sources override *stronger* ones -- the exact opposite of SS9); 6 of 12 tests failed immediately, the fix (`<=`) made all 35 guardrails tests pass. Left as a visible example of why every slice runs its full test suite before being called done, not after being trusted on read-through alone. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project) clean.
- **Slice 3 -- input guardrails** (`domain/input_guardrails.py`): the deterministic, testable part of SS10's list -- `InputLimits` (size/archive-depth/rate), `detect_secret_patterns` (four regex shapes: AWS access key, generic `key: value` assignment, PEM private-key header, JWT-like token), and `InputRateLimiter` (fixed-window, same-process). Deliberately does not attempt malware/active-content scanning (needs a real scanner engine this codebase has none of) or prompt-injection detection (its own later slice, since SS11 treats it as a distinct layer) -- scope stated plainly rather than silently claimed. `validate_input` combines all three into one `GuardrailDecision`. 20 new tests, including one confirming a denied rate-limited request does not itself count against the next window. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (53 total) clean.
- **Slice 4 -- prompt-injection guardrails** (`domain/prompt_injection.py`): `TrustedContentEnvelope` always reports `InstructionSource.RETRIEVED_OR_TOOL_PROVIDED_CONTENT` as its source (slice 2's hierarchy) -- no field on it can ever mark wrapped content as more senior, regardless of what the content itself claims. `detect_injection_signals` is a best-effort, deterministic heuristic (ten literal phrasings: "ignore previous instructions," "jailbreak," etc.) explicitly kept `ADVISORY` class, not proof of anything -- SS11 itself: "prompt-injection detection is defense in depth; authorization and tool isolation remain mandatory even when no injection is detected." 17 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (70 total) clean.
- **Slice 5 -- context guardrails** (`domain/context_guardrails.py`): `ContextItem` (SS12's "every item carries source, version, classification, scope, time, and trust state") reuses slice 3's `detect_secret_patterns` at construction time -- it simply cannot be built if its content matches a known secret shape, rather than relying on every call site to remember to check. `assemble_context_window` enforces organization/environment isolation (no cross-boundary mixing), excludes non-`CURRENT` trust states by default, and packs candidates most-recently-observed-first up to a bounded byte size -- deterministic prioritization, not a scoring model this document doesn't specify. 15 new tests, including one proving a more-recent-but-oversized item is skipped in favor of an older one that fits, not simply cut off at the first miss. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (86 total) clean.
- **Slice 6 -- retrieval guardrails** (`domain/retrieval_guardrails.py`): `filter_authorized_sources` is the load-bearing function -- it runs before any candidate becomes a visible result, so SS13's "hidden documents cannot leak through titles, counts, snippets, embeddings, or timing" holds structurally (there is no later redaction step that could itself leak something in the process of redacting it). Excludes five lifecycle states (malicious, quarantined, suspended, expired, deleted) and any organization mismatch in one pass. `bounded_retrieval` caps breadth/results; depth is documented as a caller-enforced budget this pure selection function cannot itself check without the expansion graph. `Citation`/`invalid_citations` cover SS13's "citation targets must exist, support the claim, and remain accessible to the user." 17 new tests, including a parametrized check of all five excluded lifecycle states. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (103 total) clean.
- **Slice 7 -- reasoning guardrails** (`domain/reasoning_guardrails.py`): `ReasoningClaim` closes SS14's seven-way claim taxonomy (fact/calculation/correlation/inference/hypothesis/assumption/unknown) into a type a caller must pick one of, and `ConfidenceLevel` is a three-level qualitative scale, not a numeric probability (SS14: confidence "is not fabricated as precise probability"). `has_missing_critical_evidence` and `has_causal_language` are properties, not constructor errors -- a claim with a real problem must still be constructible to be *reported* on, matching Policy Engine's own established pattern (construct first, evaluate separately) rather than raising at creation time; `evaluate_reasoning_claim` checks missing evidence before causal language, since an unevidenced claim's own phrasing is a secondary concern. 15 new tests, including one confirming a FACT claim is exempt from the causal-language check (an established fact may legitimately state a real causal relationship) while every weaker type is not. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (119 total) clean.
- **Slice 8 -- tool-use guardrails** (`domain/tool_use_guardrails.py`): `ToolCallProposal`/`ToolUseLimits`/`validate_tool_call`/`decide_tool_call` cover what is specific to a tool-call proposal itself -- tool/agent allowlist membership, typed-parameter presence, timeout/retry bounds, destination allowlist. Capability class, policy, and approval checks are explicitly left to Policy Engine (ATLAS-025) and the connector invocation-authorization path this codebase already has, rather than duplicated here. SS15: "the model receives a bounded safe denial reason and cannot retry through a different undeclared tool" -- `decide_tool_call`'s BLOCK outcome is that one bounded reason. 17 new tests covering every violation category independently and in combination. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (136 total) clean.
- **Slice 9 -- capability guardrails** (`domain/capability_guardrails.py`): SS16's AI tool-posture table, deliberately its own type rather than a re-export of Policy Engine's C0-C5 default matrix (ATLAS-025 SS11) -- that one describes what Policy *allows*; this one describes what the AI agent may ever *propose* and what Atlas may *directly invoke or dispatch*, checked before Policy is even consulted. C5 is the one class where proposal itself is denied outright ("prohibited in Atlas"), not merely execution, unlike C2-C4 which may be proposed but never directly invoked by Atlas. `posture_for` resolves an unrecognized or missing class to `None` -- SS16's "misclassified or unknown capabilities are denied until reviewed" as deny-by-absence, not a permissive fallback. 11 new tests, including exhaustive coverage of all six capability classes' proposal and invocation permissions. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (152 total) clean.
- **Slice 10 -- tool result guardrails** (`domain/tool_result_guardrails.py`): `ToolResultState` keeps SS17's "timeout, partial, unknown, and ambiguous outcomes remain distinct" as a closed enum; `normalize_result_state` accepts a model's own success claim only to prove in its signature that the parameter is never read -- SS17: "model summaries cannot change the normalized result state." `ToolResult.target_mismatch` and `requires_incident` extend SS17's "unexpected side-effect indicators stop further related calls and raise an incident" to target mismatches too (an equally serious confused-deputy signal), stated as this module's own extension since SS17 names only side effects explicitly. 15 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (167 total) clean.
- **Slice 11 -- output guardrails** (`domain/output_guardrails.py`): reuses slice 3's `detect_secret_patterns` and slice 4's `detect_injection_signals` on the output side rather than re-implementing them -- the same shapes that must never enter a prompt must never leave one either. Adds `detect_unsupported_certainty_language`, a new heuristic for SS18's "unsupported certainty, causal, safety, or success language" (six overclaiming phrasings: "guaranteed," "100% safe," "no risk," etc.). `OutputContent.missing_sections` covers SS18's required-schema check. `validate_output` combines all four into one violation list. 13 new tests, including one confirming all three detectable problems (missing section, secret, certainty language) are reported together, not just the first one found. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (182 total) clean.
- **Slice 12 -- data-loss prevention** (`domain/dlp.py`): `DlpDestinationAllowlist`/`detect_external_urls` catch model-generated URLs in output text that are not on the destination allowlist (SS19: "prevent model-generated external URLs, callbacks, or network requests from bypassing tools"). `VolumeAnomalyDetector` is the byte-volume counterpart to slice 3's request-count `InputRateLimiter`, with one deliberate behavioral difference stated plainly: it always records an access even when it pushes the running total over the limit, since SS19 is about *detecting* an anomaly in what already happened, not gatekeeping a request before it occurs. "Audit restricted export and large-volume access" is left a caller responsibility -- this module reports what should be audited, it does not write the audit record itself. 13 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (194 total) clean.

It only returns a healthy candidate whose `trust_tier` is at least the primary's own, and returns `None` (deterministic unavailability, SS20's own required outage behavior) rather than ever silently picking something less trusted, even when every candidate is unhealthy or less trusted. `ModelRequestLimits`/`is_request_within_limits` cover SS20's timeout/concurrency/retry/token bounds. 13 new tests, including one proving an unhealthy-but-more-trusted candidate is still rejected -- health and trust are independent gates, both must pass. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all guardrails test files (207 total) clean.

- **Slice 10 -- investigation presentation** (`domain/investigation_presentation.py`): `InvestigationPresentation` aggregates SS20's seven elements, reusing `ExplanationClaim`/`EvidenceLink` for the claim ledger and evidence filters rather than inventing parallel types; timeline, topology, diagnostic checks, version comparison, and related artifacts are new lightweight presentation-shape types, with a full binding to the real `health_checks`/`graph` domain objects stated plainly as a later rendering-pipeline concern. `filter_evidence_for_investigation` implements all five named filter dimensions, including "conflict" (evidence tied to a claim with contradicting evidence -- both the supporting and contradicting references, since both sides matter to a reviewer). `InvestigationAnnotation` gives SS20's "challenge a claim, add evidence, or mark a mapping issue without modifying source records" real teeth structurally: it only ever carries a `claim_id` reference plus its own identity/timestamp/note, with no field through which recording one could touch a source record; a `CLAIM_CHALLENGE` cannot construct without the `claim_id` it challenges. 16 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all explainability test files (134 total) clean.
- **Slice 11 -- reports and exports** (`domain/report_explanation.py`): discovered the existing `reports.domain.models.TechnicalReport` already models most of SS21 -- audience, generation time, source lineage/versions, classification, redaction state, reviewer status, an integrity digest, and expiry -- so `explain_report`/`ReportExplainabilityAddendum` add only what SS21 asks for beyond it (purpose, data freshness, which sections are AI-generated, excluded evidence, an access-boundary statement, and confidence/assumptions/unknowns via `ConfidenceExplanation`), bound to one exact report and version the same way `ItsmHandoffDraft` already binds to one; `explain_report` structurally rejects any `ai_generated_section_ids` not present on the report's own sections. `ExportedLink` and `OfflineExportPackage` are new, narrowly-scoped types for SS21's last two requirements (export-link re-authorization; classification/encryption/checksum/custody for offline packages), since nothing in this codebase modeled either one yet -- reusing `atlas.core.classification.DataClassification` rather than a second classification enum. 14 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all explainability test files (148 total) clean.
- **Slice 12 -- API explanation contract** (`domain/api_contract.py`): `build_api_explanation_contract` assembles SS22's eight machine-consumable fields from pieces already built across this subsystem -- `Explanation` for claims/evidence/alternatives/unknowns/source-artifact versions, `ConfidenceExplanation`, `RiskImpactExplanation`, `PolicyDenialExplanation` for policy outcome and safe reason codes -- rather than a new capture; it rejects any explanation whose channel is not `API`. SS22's "consumers must not parse prose to determine authorization or workflow state" is enforced by construction: `required_human_review` is a typed `bool` and `policy.outcome` a typed `PolicyDecisionOutcome`, never strings a consumer would need to interpret. Renderer version is left unmodeled, matching slice 1's own already-documented gap (no rendering pipeline exists yet to version). 10 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all explainability test files (154 total) clean.

SS25's "it does not silently retrain the model or alter an approved record" gets the same "reference only, never a mutation" structural treatment slice 10's `InvestigationAnnotation` already established, generalized to all seven actions rather than that type's narrower investigation-view subset of three. `resulting_artifact_kind` makes "feedback creates a new artifact or review item" a checkable, non-optional field. `__post_init__` enforces the two cross-field invariants: a claim-quality complaint cannot construct without the `claim_id` it targets, and `field_correction` can be present if and only if `kind is CORRECTION_SUPPLIED`. 15 new tests. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy` (full project), and all explainability test files (169 total) clean.

- **What this is**: `mcp/connectors/huawei_pacific/source-provenance.json` stated plainly that
  `oam_agent_status`, `error_code`, and `warranty_status` are real, confirmed OceanStor Pacific
  node fields (confirmed via the same real, independently-maintained Icinga/Nagios check-plugin
  source that confirmed every other field this connector uses) that the health mapping simply
  never surfaced. Closed for real, not just documented as a known gap.
- **Domain model** (`backend/src/atlas/modules/connectors/vendors/huawei_pacific/domain.py`):
  added all three as optional (`str | None`) fields on `HuaweiPacificClusterNode`, explicitly
  *not* mapped into a guessed status enum the way `running_status` is -- the shared monitoring
  library that confirmed `running_status`'s exact `'online'`/`'offline'` vocabulary (by reading
  its `get_node_running_status_state()` function directly) has no equivalent function for these
  three, so inventing a vocabulary for them would be guessing, not confirming.
- **Client parsing** (`client.py`): added a defensive `_optional_str` helper -- these are the
  first genuinely optional fields on this node type (every other field is required and fails the
  whole node read if malformed); absence or an unrecognized shape is treated as unavailable
  (`None`), not a parse failure, since only the four already-required fields were confirmed
  present on every node the reference plugin reads.
- **Health mapping** (`backend/src/atlas/modules/health_checks/adapters/huawei_pacific.py`): each
  present field becomes its own `HealthObservation` (`node.oam_agent_status`,
  `node.warranty_status`, `node.error_code`). `oam_agent_status` and `warranty_status` are
  reported `ObservationState.UNKNOWN` and never drive a finding -- their vocabulary is genuinely
  unconfirmed, and asserting severity from it would be fabricating meaning the source doesn't
  support. `error_code` is the one defensible exception: a present, non-`"0"`/non-empty value is
  surfaced as `WARNING` (not `CRITICAL` -- the mapping from code to actual severity is still
  unconfirmed) and generates a finding, matching this exact connector's own established
  convention for interpreting vendor "code" fields (`client.py`'s `_bounded()` already treats a
  non-zero/non-`"0"` `result.code` as a logical error the same way).
- **Tests**: `test_huawei_pacific_connector.py` gained a dedicated test confirming these three
  fields parse when present and resolve to `None` when a node omits them (not a malformed-read
  failure). `test_configured_huawei_pacific_health_executor.py` gained a test confirming all
  three observations appear with the right `state`, and that a non-zero `error_code` produces
  exactly one `WARNING` finding referencing the raw code value.
- **Docs kept honest**: `source-provenance.json`'s `unconfirmed_gaps` and `README.md` no longer
  claim these fields are unsurfaced; both now state precisely what *is* surfaced (raw,

### ATLAS-IMP-274 Scope and Verification

- **What this is**: a full-repository survey (prompted by the user's "keep going until the whole
  project is done, you decide" instruction) found that CI's backend job had been silently failing
  since commit `db68c5e0` (several tasks prior in this same session) -- every run failed at the
  "Migrate PostgreSQL integration database" step, with everything after it skipped. Confirmed
  directly via the GitHub Actions API (`gh` was unavailable in this environment; used the public
  `api.github.com/repos/.../actions/runs` REST endpoints instead) before touching anything: this
  wasn't a hypothesis, it was an already-failing, unaddressed CI state.
- **Root cause**: migration `20260827_0169` runs `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector`
  unconditionally, both in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s Postgres service container and in
  `compose.yaml`'s backend service startup command (`alembic upgrade head` on every
  `docker compose up`) -- both were pointed at vanilla `postgres` images (`postgres:17`,
  `postgres:18.4-alpine`), which do not ship the `vector` extension.
- **Fix**: switched both to the pgvector project's own official image
  (`pgvector/pgvector:pg17`, `pgvector/pgvector:pg18`) -- confirmed via the image's own
  documentation to be the official postgres image plus the extension binary, run identically,
  with `CREATE EXTENSION` still required explicitly (which the migration already does) -- a
  verified drop-in replacement, not a workaround.
- **Verified against real CI, not just locally, twice**: run #1024 (the immediately following
  commit, ADR-IMP-275's index rebuild) completed with every single step green, including the
  final catch-all `pytest -n 4 --dist loadfile` step -- confirmed by reading the full per-step
  job breakdown via the Actions API, not just the top-level conclusion.

### ATLAS-IMP-273 Scope and Verification

- **What this is**: this local Windows machine had never actually run its ~69 `ATLAS_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN`-gated tests -- they always self-skipped for lack of a configured database. With a local PostgreSQL 18 instance and a dedicated `atlas_test_user` role set up, running them for real surfaced three distinct issues, none of them in application code.
- **Root cause 1 (real code fix, the only one requiring a change to a tracked file)**: Windows' default `asyncio` event loop policy is the proactor policy, but psycopg's async driver only implements the selector-based transport, so every async Postgres test failed with `psycopg.InterfaceError: Psycopg cannot use the 'ProactorEventLoop' to run in async mode`. This project's actual CI target (`ubuntu-latest`, see `.github/workflows/ci.yml`) never hits this since POSIX event loops are already selector-based. Fixed in `backend/tests/conftest.py`: `asyncio.set_event_loop_policy(asyncio.WindowsSelectorEventLoopPolicy())`, guarded to `sys.platform == "win32"` only, following the same pattern as ATLAS-IMP-272's `tmp_path` fix. Confirmed nothing in this codebase's async tests uses `asyncio.create_subprocess_*` (the one capability the proactor policy adds), so the switch is safe.
- **Root cause 2 (local environment setup, not a code issue)**: several migration round-trip tests use `SET LOCAL session_replication_role = replica` to bypass triggers while seeding legacy fixture rows, a Postgres superuser-only operation. CI's `atlas` role is a fresh superuser by default (Docker Postgres service container); the local `atlas_test_user` role was not, and was granted `SUPERUSER` to match.
- **Root cause 3 (my own setup mistake, corrected, not a code issue)**: initially ran the entire suite as one `pytest -n 4 --dist loadfile` against a single shared database. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` does not do this -- it isolates schema-mutating test groups (ones that call `alembic downgrade`/`upgrade` on the shared schema, or use fixed hardcoded IDs for deterministic race-condition tests) into **five separate databases**, run **sequentially**, with the generic parallel run only covering everything else (with no `ATLAS_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN` set at all, so Postgres-gated tests correctly self-skip there). Replicated CI's exact topology locally: `atlas_test`, `atlas_process_creation_test`, `atlas_downstream_test`, `atlas_review_request_test`, `atlas_reviewer_assignment_test`, each migrated and exercised by the same file groups and DSNs `ci.yml` uses.
- **Verified with the real toolchain, matching CI's job structure exactly** (all Postgres databases migrated to `20260827_0168` -- the revision immediately before the pgvector-dependent one, since pgvector is not installed on this machine): every CI-parity step passed cleanly except the tests that specifically call `alembic upgrade(config, "head")` inside the test body -- those fail on `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector` (a genuine, already-known, environment-only gap, not masked or worked around). One further effect traced and confirmed non-independent: `test_invocation_evidence.py::test_live_postgres_invocation_evidence_isolates_same_identifiers_by_tenant` fails immediately after `test_bounded_invocation.py`'s migration round-trip test in the same file group -- because that test's `try/finally` calls `command.upgrade(config, "head")` in *both* the try body and the `finally` cleanup, and both fail identically (pgvector), the schema is left stuck at the downgraded `20260824_0161` revision instead of restored, so the next test runs against pre-tenant-scoping tables. This is a downstream consequence of the same single pgvector gap, not a fourth independent bug -- confirmed by tracing the exact migration-log output, not assumed. Final full-suite catch-all step (no DSN set, matching `ci.yml`'s last job step exactly): **4046 passed, 69 skipped, 0 failed** -- identical to ATLAS-IMP-272's clean baseline, confirming the event-loop fix caused no regression anywhere else.

### ATLAS-IMP-272 Scope and Verification

- **What this is**: every prior task in this series ran the full backend suite before committing
  and reported "matches the established ~67-failure baseline, all pre-existing and unrelated" --
  true in the sense that none of those tasks caused the failures, but the baseline itself was
  never actually diagnosed. Asked to prioritize and finish outstanding work, this task
  investigated and closed it completely: **0 failures remain**.
- **Root cause 1 (the large majority, ~62 of 67)**: Windows' 260-character `MAX_PATH` limit.
  Pytest's own default temp-dir naming (`%TEMP%\pytest-of-<user>\pytest-<N>\<test-name><index>`)
  stacked on this project's real, legitimate deep content-addressed storage paths (e.g.
  `deployments/<org>/<env>/<site>/<release>/.../<64-char digest>/target...`) routinely exceeds
  260 characters on this local Windows machine. Confirmed by exact character-counting the failing
  paths (one measured at precisely 260, several others 263-285) and by confirming this project's
  CI runs exclusively on `ubuntu-latest` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`), so this never manifested
  there. Two distinct symptoms of the same limit were found and both handled: outright
  `WinError 3`/`WinError 206` on `mkdir`/`rename`, and a *silent* one -- `Path.is_file()` and
  `Path.exists()` swallow the `OSError` from a failing `stat()` call on an over-length path and
  return `False`, so `bootstrap_integrations_filesystem.py`'s `inspect()` (and its siblings)
  raised a business-logic-looking `bootstrap_integration_unknown_target` error even though the
  file was genuinely present on disk (confirmed by direct post-run filesystem inspection).
- **Fix (test-only, zero production-code changes)**: new `backend/tests/conftest.py` overrides
  pytest's `tmp_path` fixture on `sys.platform == "win32"` only (every other platform, including
  CI, is untouched) to wrap the path in Windows' `\\?\` extended-length prefix, which makes
  Windows accept paths up to ~32,767 characters and bypasses `MAX_PATH` entirely -- with no
  machine-wide registry change (`LongPathsEnabled`) required, which would have been
  inappropriate to make unilaterally. Confirmed correct through `resolve()`, `mkdir()`,
  `rename()`, `is_file()`, `rglob()`, and `relative_to()` via a standalone script before wiring
  it into the fixture, since `pathlib`'s handling of `\\?\`-prefixed paths has historically been
  inconsistent across Python versions.
- **Root cause 2 (5 tests)**: `test_alembic_graph_has_single_0150_head` and four siblings each
  assert `script.get_heads() == ["20260827_0168"]` as a "the migration graph is still
  single-headed (no accidental branch), and here's the current tip" sanity check, alongside an
  unrelated, still-valid lineage assertion for a specific older revision named in each test's own
  title. A real, already-committed, correctly-linear migration
  (`20260827_0169_document_knowledge_vectors.py`, `down_revision = "20260827_0168"`, part of the
  earlier ATLAS-IMP-256 document-knowledge work) advanced the true head, and these five assertions
  were never bumped to match. Verified the graph is still genuinely single-headed
  (`script.get_heads() == ["20260827_0169"]`, confirmed via a direct Alembic `ScriptDirectory`
  query) before updating -- this is a real, no-branching, linear graph, not a masked bug.
- **Verified with the real toolchain**: `ruff format --check .`, `ruff check .`, and `mypy` strict
  clean across the full repository. Full backend suite:
  **4046 passed, 69 skipped, 0 failed** (0:24:24) -- versus the immediately prior run's 3980
  passed / 67 failed / 68 skipped. The failure count fully explains the delta: 66 of the 67
  former failures now pass, and the 67th now reaches a legitimate, pre-existing
  `symlink creation is not available on this Windows host` skip in
  `test_bootstrap_artifact_acquisition.py` that an earlier MAX_PATH failure had been masking
  (accounting for the skip count's +1). This is the first fully clean backend suite run across
  this entire multi-session connector engagement.

### ATLAS-IMP-268 Scope and Verification

- **What this closes**: ATLAS-IMP-266 shipped vCenter's graph adapter entities-only, naming two
  relationship gaps explicitly: host-to-cluster membership and VM-to-host placement, both left
  unmodeled because the plain `GET /api/vcenter/host`/`/cluster`/`/vm` list responses carry no
  parent-cluster or running-host field on either side. This task investigates both gaps properly
  (not from memory -- fresh research) and closes the one that turned out to be genuinely
  resolvable with confirmed real API mechanisms.
- **Host-to-cluster membership: resolvable, and now real**. `Host.FilterSpec` (confirmed in
  ATLAS-IMP-266 from VMware's own generated Python client source) has a `clusters` field --
  re-confirmed this task, quoting the source docstring directly: `"Clusters that must contain the
  hosts for the hosts to match the filter... identifiers for the resource type:
  ClusterComputeResource."` This means `GET /api/vcenter/host?filter.clusters=<cluster_id>` is a
  real, confirmed, bounded way to resolve exactly which hosts belong to a given cluster.
  `VCenterClient.read_cluster_membership()` calls it once per cluster (bounded to the first 25
  clusters; additional clusters are named as a completeness gap, not silently dropped), and
  `ConfiguredVCenterGraphSnapshotProvider` emits a real `HYPERVISOR_HOST --DEPENDS_ON-->
  HYPERVISOR_CLUSTER` relationship per confirmed membership -- the first connector-backed graph
  relationship built in this entire multi-vendor connector series (every prior real graph adapter
  -- Hitachi, Brocade, Dorado, Pacific, and vCenter's own first pass -- shipped entities-only).
- **VM-to-host placement: investigated properly, confirmed still genuinely unresolvable, not
  guessed**. The VM detail response's complete field list was re-confirmed this task directly
  from the official Ansible `vmware.vmware_rest` collection's machine-generated
  `vcenter_vm_info` module documentation (generated from the same real vSphere Automation API
  definitions used throughout this connector): `boot, boot_devices, cdroms, cpu, disks, floppies,
  guest_OS, hardware, identity, instant_clone_frozen, memory, name, nics, nvme_adapters,
  parallel_ports, power_state, sata_adapters, scsi_adapters, serial_ports` -- no host, cluster, or
  placement field appears anywhere in that list. A separate real, official Postman collection for
  this API (`vsphere-automation-sdk-rest`, archived but authoritative) was also checked and
  contains no example response demonstrating a VM-to-host field either. This gap is confirmed
  genuine, not merely unconfirmed by omission, and is left exactly as stated rather than
  fabricated with a guessed field name.
- **Fail-safe, not fail-closed, for the new membership reads**: a membership-read failure for one
  cluster (transport fault, malformed response) is caught per-cluster and recorded as a known
  gap, not allowed to discard the already-successful host/cluster/VM entity reads by failing the
  whole snapshot -- the same graceful-degradation philosophy Brocade's per-fabric fault reads
  established. A membership result naming a host id absent from the same snapshot's host
  inventory (a live-read race, in principle) is also caught and omitted rather than asserted
  against a nonexistent entity, which `GraphSnapshot`'s own validation would otherwise reject.
- **A real transport capability gap found and fixed along the way**: `VCenterHttpsTransport`'s
  path validator rejected any query string at all (the three original list reads never needed
  one). Widened to accept one bounded `key=value` query parameter, mirroring the exact pattern
  `BrocadeSanNavHttpsTransport` already established for its fault/events endpoint.
- **Verified with the real toolchain**: `ruff format --check` and `ruff check` clean across the
  full repository (1792 files); `mypy` strict clean across every touched file. New tests: 2 for
  the connector package (real membership-field parsing via the confirmed filter, unsafe-identifier
  rejection), 2 net-new for the graph adapter (graceful degradation when the membership route is
  unavailable, safe omission of a membership host absent from inventory -- the third relevant
  test replaced the prior entities-only assertion in place rather than adding a new one) -- 4 new
  tests total, all passing alongside the 24 pre-existing vCenter tests (28 total, all green).
  Targeted multi-area sweep (`-k "vcenter or graph or connector or commvault or hitachi or
  brocade or huawei"`): 352 passed, 5 failed, all baseline alembic-head-drift, zero overlap.
  Full backend suite: 3956 passed, 67 failed, 68 skipped -- the failure count matches the
  established ~67 pre-existing baseline exactly, confirmed by name to share zero overlap with
  vcenter, graph, connector, or any vendor module. The pass-count increase (+4 over
  ATLAS-IMP-267's 3952) matches exactly the 4 new tests this task adds.

### ATLAS-IMP-267 Scope and Verification

- **What this is**: the sixth and final real vendor connector -- Commvault CommServe is a backup
  platform, closing the fifth and last vendor explicitly named in the original request (Brocade
  SANnav, Huawei Dorado, Huawei Pacific, vCenter, Commvault). All five are now real,
  connector-backed, and wired into at least one consuming module.
- **Deliberately scoped narrower than the storage/hypervisor vendors, and why**: the plan
  document itself flagged Commvault as needing "a new module... for job/policy/recovery-point
  domain concepts that don't exist anywhere in this codebase today -- the largest of the five."
  Rather than design and build a new `backup_operations` domain module speculatively in the same
  session, this task takes the same incremental-slice approach already proven for every other
  vendor (Brocade shipped health_checks+graph first, RCA later; Dorado/Pacific shipped
  storage+graph+health_checks first, RCA/recommendations later): it ships the single most
  valuable, lowest-risk, most clearly-scoped piece -- a real backup job-status health signal --
  using the existing, already-vendor-agnostic `HealthCheckDefinition`/`HealthObservation`/
  `HealthCheckFinding` domain model, which needed no changes at all (the same fact already
  established for Brocade in ATLAS-IMP-261). No new module, no graph entities, no storage
  overview, no RCA/recommendations -- named explicitly as out of scope, not silently dropped.
- **Real API research**: confirmed via Commvault's own official documentation across two
  independent pages, including a literal, complete example JSON response on the official
  api.commvault.com machine-generated reference (`GET /webservice/Job` returning
  `{"totalRecordsWithoutPaging": N, "jobs": [{"jobSummary": {"jobId", "status", "jobType",
  "percentComplete", "subclientName", "destClientName", "subclient": {"clientName", ...}}}]}`).
  Login (`POST webservice/Login`, body `{username, password (Base64), domain, commserver,
  timeout}`, response field `"token"`) and the subsequent-request header were each confirmed from
  Commvault's own documentation.commvault.com page and independently corroborated by a second,
  separate official page (api.commvault.com's AuthenticationOperations/Login reference).
- **A real, confirmed difference from every other connector built this session**: the session
  token is presented on every subsequent request via a header literally named `Authtoken` -- not
  `X-Auth-Token` (both Huawei connectors), not `vmware-api-session-id` (vCenter), not
  `Authorization: Bearer`/`Basic` (Hitachi, Brocade). `CommvaultHttpsTransport` still performs the
  same complete, bounded login -> read -> logout cycle for every single `get()` call as every
  other session-based connector this session, for the same reason: no session ever outlives one
  bounded operation.
- **Honest enum-vocabulary limitation, stated plainly rather than guessed**: Commvault's own
  documentation states its complete job-status vocabulary is longer than what could be
  independently confirmed via real, working examples during connector construction. Only the
  values directly evidenced across real sources (`Completed`, `Running`, `Waiting`, `Suspended`,
  `Killed`) are modeled in `CommvaultJobStatus`; any other value (e.g. a specific
  partial-success or failure-reason status Commvault is known to have) maps to `UNKNOWN` rather
  than being assigned a guessed severity -- the same rigor already established for Huawei
  Pacific's `running_status` and Dorado's `HEALTHSTATUS`.
- **New health-check mapping**: `CommvaultJobHealthExecutor` maps job status to observation state
  (`Completed`/`Running`/`Waiting` -> NORMAL, `Suspended` -> WARNING, `Killed` -> CRITICAL,
  unrecognized -> UNKNOWN), a new per-vendor mapping table, following the same "a finding alone
  does not force PARTIAL, only an incomplete collection does" rule established by every prior
  configured health executor (Dorado, Pacific, vCenter).
- **Wiring**: `api/app.py`'s health_checks executor fallback chain now runs Hitachi -> Brocade ->
  Huawei Dorado -> Huawei Pacific -> vCenter -> Commvault -> Synthetic, the longest chain built
  this session. `InventoryDeviceType.BACKUP` already existed in `modules/inventory` (added in an
  earlier phase, confirmed unused until now), so the allowlist check needed no inventory-domain
  change -- only a vendor-substring check (`"commvault" in device.vendor.lower()`), the same
  pattern used for every other vendor's allowlist.
- **Verified with the real toolchain**: `ruff format --check` and `ruff check` clean across the
